message.content:
The most iconic sculpture that people often associate with the late‑19th‑century artistic milieu is **Auguste Rodin’s “The Thinker.”**  Although Rodin began the work in 1880 and the bronze version was cast in 1902, the piece was conceived and largely completed during the 1880s, making it a product of the 19th‑century sculptural tradition.  It has become a cultural shorthand for modern sculpture and is frequently cited as the most famous sculpture of that era.

Other 19th‑century works that rival its fame include:

| Sculpture | Artist | Year | Why it matters |
|-----------|--------|------|----------------|
| **“The Kiss”** | Rodin | 1889 | A masterful study of intimacy and movement; it was exhibited at the 1889 Exposition Universelle in Paris. |
| **“The Gates of Hell”** | Rodin | 1880–1917 (unfinished) | An ambitious monumental project that influenced generations of sculptors. |
| **“The Burghers of Calais”** | Rodin | 1889 | A powerful allegory of sacrifice and civic duty. |
| **“The Rape of the Sabine Women”** | Antonio Canova | 1797–1807 | Though early 19th‑century, it set a new standard for neoclassical drama. |

If you’re looking for a single answer, “The Thinker” is the most widely recognized and celebrated sculpture that emerged from the 19th‑century sculptural movement.
